ios.desc:
ParaGraFX is an EPUB reader that illustrates the page you are actually on. Stop on any passage and generate an image drawn from that specific moment in the text — not a generic cover, not the author's portrait, but the scene in front of you.

THIRTY-SEVEN STYLES, OR INVENT YOUR OWN
Not thirty-seven kinds of oil painting: the styles span the ways pictures get made. Gothic stained glass, Japanese woodblock, Victorian pen-and-ink engraving, Byzantine mosaic, medieval illuminated manuscript, linocut, risograph, cyanotype blueprint, cross-stitch sampler, Art Deco poster, Bauhaus geometry, Memphis postmodern, Silver Age comic book, plasticine stop-motion, anime cel, 16-bit pixel art, teletext blocks, Italian Futurism, brutalist concrete, neon synthwave — and more. Or describe a style of your own, anything you can put into words. Your styles are saved and appear everywhere you generate. Four of the most demanding styles appear once Image Quality is set to Standard or higher, because the fast renderer cannot draw them properly.

REFINE WHAT YOU GET
Ask for a change in plain words — warmer light, night-time, more detail — or edit the image prompt directly and send exactly what you wrote.

A HUNDRED AND NINETY-SIX CLASSICS, ONE TAP AWAY
Pride and Prejudice, Jane Eyre, Frankenstein, Crime and Punishment, Moby-Dick, The Great Gatsby, Dracula, The Odyssey, Mrs Dalloway, Madame Bovary, Treasure Island, The Secret Garden, Macbeth, Les Misérables — browse them by shelf or by letter, search by title or author, and tap one to start reading. Most arrive in a second or two. Two are already inside the app, so a first run works with no signal at all, and nothing else is downloaded until you ask for it.

Fifty-two of them are ancient and medieval: Herodotus and Thucydides, Aeschylus, Aristophanes and Euripides, Lucretius and Tacitus, the Argonautica and the Golden Ass, the Prose and Poetic Eddas, the Mabinogion, Le Morte d'Arthur, the Kalevala and the Tale of Genji — in translations whose copyright has expired, each one opened and read in the app before it went on the shelf.

BRING YOUR OWN BOOKS
Open any EPUB from Files, or search Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks and the Internet Archive from inside the app — seventy-five thousand more books, beyond the shelf.

ILLUSTRATE A WHOLE BOOK
Queue every chapter at once and let it work in the background — each chapter gets its own illustration, in a style you pick or one you invent.

A PROPER READER
Adjustable type, a hundred colour

quotes.text:
A few years ago when Stable Diffusion was released, I happened to be reading Homer's Iliad and came across a section where Achilles' shield is described in great detail. I fed the passage into Stable Diffusion, wondering how well it would do in creating an illustration of the shield. Of course it was terrible, but a year later DALL-E 3 seemed to do a pretty good job, as long as you didn't look too hard at the details. By then I had been reading Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (yes I had been on a classics binge), and created a Python app that let me feed random paragraphs into DALL-E 3. The results were often grand collages that seemed to look like a combination of Renaissance art and graffiti.

After playing around with this idea for a bit, I realized it would be pretty cool to have a dedicated app that could download public-domain books and illustrate them with DALL-E 3. I have been working on this idea for a few years, at first copying code back and forth from Xcode to the ChatGPT prompt, and then later using Claude Code. I didn't know anything about developing for the iPhone, and had to tackle a broad range of issues, everything from setting up a serverless backend to writing code in Swift to releasing an app on the App Store. Technical issues as mundane as how to parse an EPUB correctly or how to create an engaging UI/UX were surprisingly complex.
